name: Fibrous plaster (moulding plaster)
summary: A thin laminate made in the workshop: a face coat of plaster of Paris cast against a mould, backed by layers of hessian (jute scrim) soaked in plaster and stiffened with timber laths. The moulds are taken from models whose profiles were run with a zinc template, so a cornice arrives as straight lengths that are fixed on site, with corners and returns cut and made up there. It is the Rotunda's entablature, archivolts, imposts, niche surrounds and sills.
faceNote: Everything a visitor sees is the plaster of Paris face coat, so optics, luminous reflectance and surface histories are the face substance's; this record holds only what the laminate adds (reinforcement, stock, fixing, failure).

formation.how: A flexible or plaster mould is taken from a run or modelled original. The face coat is poured or brushed into it, hessian scrim dipped in plaster is laid behind in two or more layers, and sawn timber laths and ribs are bedded in to stiffen the back. When set the cast is lifted, and lengths are fixed on site by wads (strips of plaster-soaked hessian tied round the structure above) or by screws and metalwork.

history.text: The modern method was patented in 1856 by the French modeller Leonard Alexander Desachy, drawing on a Parisian recipe (Harrison); lighter than solid plaster, easily reinforced and cheap to make in ornate designs, it quickly became popular with homeowners, theatre and music hall owners, and architects (Clifford).

corners.text: Sections of runs are cut for corners, mitres and awkward returns and fixed with nails or screws, fresh plaster serving as the adhesive; where a running mould cannot reach (its sledge has a length), the last part of a run is finished by hand.
corners.source: Who's Been Living in My House? Kemp Town Estate histories, Plasterwork (2015), https://www.kemptownestatehistories.com/plasterwork; Vadstrup, S., Working techniques and repair methods for plaster decorations on facades: running mould decorations. Plaster Architecture project essay, https://www.palazzospinelli.org/plaster/essay/essay/Soren06.html

handFinishedRunEnd.asReported: the last 10 cm at the end of the running mould decoration made 'by hand'

photograph: Long straight members with a perfectly continuous profile, broken about every 3 m by the joint between two cast lengths, which reads as a hairline or a faint change of texture.
Mitres at corners slightly softer and less regular than the run lengths, because they were finished by hand.
The face is plaster of Paris: matt, fine, sometimes with pinholes; soiling lies on the upward faces of cornices and in the quirks and fillets.
Hairline cracks along joints and at fixings; in old ceilings, sagging or cracks where wads have failed.
